title: The teacher and lineage
hookLine: a Tibetan teacher reads a text aloud to students who could read it themselves, and that's the point

cards: A room full of students, each with a copy of the text. Every one of them can read.
And yet a teacher at the front reads the whole thing aloud, quickly, sometimes so fast it's hard to follow, from the first line to the last. Nobody takes notes. Nobody asks questions.
From the back of the room it can look like a strange use of an afternoon.
But in Tibetan Buddhism, something is being handed over that isn't on the page: permission, connection, a living link back through the people who read it to the people who read it to this teacher.

teach.b: Back on day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven, Zen showed us the teacher face to face. Tibetan Buddhism puts the teacher at the center too, in its own shape. First, the teacher.

In Tibetan the word is lama, used for the Sanskrit guru. Tibetan texts treat the teacher as the doorway to practice, the one who makes the teaching alive for a particular student. Second, the reading.
What happened in that room is called a lung, a reading transmission: the text read aloud so it's received by ear from someone who received it the same way. Third, empowerment.

Some Tibetan practices, especially visualizing a buddha or reciting certain mantras, are begun only after an empowerment, a ceremony in which a qualified teacher introduces the student to that practice.
Some texts and practices stay closed until then. Not secret for the sake of it, the tradition says, but because without guidance they can be misunderstood. Fourth, the lineage.

teach.h: A CHAIN OF PEOPLE, AND CARE.
teach.b: Each practice is said to come down an unbroken chain, teacher to student, and lineages have prayers that name the chain one person at a time. Practicing means stepping into that line.

And the tradition keeps a balance: Tibetan texts on finding a teacher warn the student to examine a teacher carefully, sometimes for a long time, before trusting them. Respect and care belong together.
Some things can be learned from a book. Some can't.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, students receive a practice from a teacher through a reading transmission, an empowerment and instructions, and lineages recite prayers naming the teachers who passed it down.

games.why: some Tibetan practices are begun only after an empowerment from a qualified teacher, so they're understood rightly.

practice: Bring to mind something you've been trying to learn alone, from books or videos: an instrument, a language, a way of prayer or meditation. Where does it keep stalling?

Then ask the question the Tibetan texts ask: if a guide were to help with this, what would you want to see in them before trusting them, patience, honesty, their own practice? Don't decide anything; let the question sit.

wordCard.voice: The teacher and lineage. In Tibetan Buddhism, the lama who gives the reading and the empowerment, and the chain of teachers behind them. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan bla ma: teacher, used for the Sanskrit guru.

carryVoice: Your line: some things need a teacher. And a teacher is worth examining before you trust one. Go gently.
